definition: In this historical classification of aphasia, subcortical aphasia is a form distinguished from cortical and transcortical aphasia. The passage links it with dyslalia, meaning a disorder centered more narrowly on spoken speech output than on language processes in general.

reasons: The packet supports that subcortical, cortical, and transcortical aphasia are distinguished in a historical classification, and that subcortical corresponds to dyslalia.
The claim that dyslalia means a disorder centered more narrowly on spoken speech output than on language processes in general is not supported by the packet and adds an unsupported interpretation.

The packet supports that there is a classification distinguishing “cortical” from “subcortical” aphasia and discusses “transcortical” aphasia as a related controversy, but it does not clearly state that “subcortical aphasia is a form distinguished from cortical and transcortical aphasia” in the way the definition phrases it.

The packet links subcortical/transcortical/cortical categories to dyslogia/dysphasia and mentions “dyslalia” in connection with this classification, but it does not define dyslalia as “a disorder centered more narrowly on spoken speech output than on language processes in general,” nor provide that comparison.
